utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We have now finished with the pleas of the accused, so I think that we should now have a very brief Status Conference. The first thing that I should say, for the benefit of Mr. Lukic, is that the time limit of 15 days that you have requested starts as of today. Thank you very much for this gift in terms of time limits. Now let us see how we stand in terms of housekeeping matters and practical issues. I don't know whether my colleagues wish to have a break at this point? No. I think would can, therefore, continue. Ms. Somers has informed the Chamber that discovery process has been going on and that it has not been affected by the motion to amend the indictment in any way. So I should perhaps give her the floor so that we can see where we stand regarding the preparation of the case, and perhaps optimistically - although I want a realistic answer - whether she can tell us if we are able to finish this preparatory phase of the proceedings before the 16th of November. So two questions: how we stand, and whether the pre-trial phase is likely to be completed before the 16th of November.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. The Prosecution's obligations pursuant to Rule 66(A) are complete. The Prosecution has undertaken to provide in advance of any initiative by the Defence a number of the documentary exhibits which it will seek to use in the course of the Prosecution's case, and we are continuously, or continually, sending these out as - well, of course, translations are not necessarily required now - so as we have them ready. The issue that may have some impact upon whether or not we could meet the Chamber's hopeful deadline would include some matters such as adjudicated facts. Mr. Lukic and I have spoken about this. We are hoping to meet hopefully within the next two weeks, depending also on his staffing situation - he has indicated to the Chamber he has some concerns, and he has shared those with me - his staff and my staff, to iron out a number of adjudicated facts of which this Chamber or its successor Chamber, but hopefully this Chamber may take judicial notice to avoid bringing back a parade of witnesses for both historical background facts as well as perhaps even some of the other factual issues that have arisen in the course of both the Kvocka-Omarska, and Sikirica-Keraterm cases, as well as Tadic. I am optimistic that although this is a political leadership case and a heavy document case, that we can find agreement on a number of these points as it is, in my view, in the interests of all parties not to have to waste the Chamber's time with quite a bit of live testimony. We have discussed numbers of witnesses more or less in the preliminary phase, and we are moving ahead toward a 65 ter-type of status. Both my learned friend opposite and I have sought at this point to request - although he has a bit of time, I must make the initial request - for a variance on page numbers for this pre-trial brief because of the need to explain a number of the points which will come out in documents which we believe is in the interests of the Chamber to have right up front rather than have to seek additional or collateral information. It would, I think, help to have it explained in the course of our case. So rather than both of us having asked, we will be asking verbally, and if the Chamber wishes, we can do so in writing for an additional maximum 50 pages, maximum total 100, exclusive of any annexes which we may find helpful to the Chamber. The processes leading to the dates -- I'm a little bit unable to estimate time for, if -- if we knew, for example, approximate dates that were in mind for a trial, I think we might be able to give a better estimation. Both counsel and I have discussed our hope that this trial may start after the first quarter of the year so that as many issues as can be stipulated to or better identified are done so. Again, as a document case, in my view, it probably would run more smoothly. Although it seems that asking for more time might be an inconvenience administratively, it is our belief in good faith in the long run it will save time. If the Chamber could assist both of us in perhaps knowing from the time of receipt of the 72 motions, I believe we would have, if I'm correct - I'll ask my colleague - seven days in which to respond, and depending on -- I know this is a heavily burdened Chamber now, there are a number of matters pending, but if this Chamber were able to resolve issues raised by 72, and allow us to move quickly enough, bearing in mind its heavy burdens and obligations, we would try then, with no interruption, to move on to the next phase. The Chamber would designate to us its timetable, as is permitted in the Rules. So we offer and we pledge our full cooperation, mindful of the fact that we are trying to -- not to start, if possible, any earlier than the end of the first quarter of next year, if this is -- if this can be accommodated. We have discussed, again, rough witness numbers. We have discussed the desire, where appropriate, to use 92 bis, where appropriate. We have discussed ruling out certain matters provided for in the Rules, such as deposition. We do not find it particularly advantageous on time. We think that perhaps the mechanism of the judicially noticed facts will speed along. Those, of course, must be looked at very carefully. Some of the matters which were perhaps easier to address in a case such as the Omarska case may be more difficult in a political leadership case; however, we are fully prepared to work on the mutually-arrived-at, guided-by-the-Chamber timetable.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. Thank you, Ms. Susan Somers. I am going to hear Mr. Lukic and then put forward some of my own ideas. Mr. Lukic, let's hear how things stand, or do you have any comments to make in response to what Ms. Somers has just said? And perhaps we can take the second point first. If you don't want to respond, that's fine. Are you going to make any preliminary motions and, if so, which? But as I say, if you don't wish to respond, that's all right as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, I can respond. We are making two preliminary motions. One is a motion objecting to the form of the indictment; and one more. And my learned colleague correctly explained to this Chamber all aspects we discussed among each other, and I don't think that it's necessary to explain anything more. Only I want to explain my part, why I ask for this trial not to begin at least before the second quarter of the next year. I know that this is not the question which should be raised in front of this Trial Chamber, but only two days ago, I had only one investigator, and that's my team. So I have some problems with the Registrar composing my Defence team, and I cannot promise that we can - if we work in this pace - that we can be very efficient. So I think that I need at least three or even four investigators and that I need a co-counsel, even in this phase. So I think that from my stand, it's very optimistic that this Defence team will be ready for trial before the second quarter of next year.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well, Mr. Lukic. Thank you. I think that the new rules of the Registry and Registrar with respect to appointment of counsel will perhaps allow you to have your team as soon as possible, because it is quite clear to us all that the pre-trial stage must be got through as soon as possible. I think we have a new philosophy now, not to prolong the pre-trial phase. But with the ad litem Judges, we have changed our way of thinking; that is, to get through the pre-trial proceedings as soon as possible and not to go into it for days and days and months and months in preparation of a case, in getting it trial-ready. We have to finish this -- these pre-trial proceedings as soon as possible and become trial-ready as soon as possible and to tap all the necessary human resources towards that end. So I think that you might just be getting some good news very soon. Another point that I wanted to make is the following: When I talked to and asked whether it was optimistic to set the 16th of November as a deadline date for the pre-trial matters, it was with a view to the trial. But I'm asking you for a realistic date as well, optimistic and realistic. I wanted this date to be the end of the date for the pre-trial phase, but according to this Chamber and its schedule, it should be trial-ready towards February next. So what I can tell you here and now is that we're going to wait for the preliminary motions to be filed by the Defence and then we can make up an agenda, calendar, for our work, to work towards the deadlines. And I'm telling the Prosecution and the Defence now that the Chamber, Trial Chamber, is ready for a fixed date for the trial to go ahead. I think that the Prosecution should make an effort to stabilise the indictment. And when I use this term, what I want to say is that the accused -- that the indictment must be our instrument of work. That is my personal opinion, and I'm speaking in my own name. Otherwise, we won't be able to programme Status Conferences. So the Tribunal must enter into a stage when our work will have to be programmed with Status Conferences, and we can't do that unless we keep having amendments and corrigendums and so on and so forth. So I think we must focus on that point and organise our work accordingly. As you know, the Tribunal is going to go ahead with six trials a day simultaneously, so we cannot make mistakes in programming and organisation. We have to programme and we have an organise. And having said this, we have to fix a calendar as soon as we see the preliminary motions filed by the Defence. And as the Pre-Trial Judge, I will set the a calendar, working calendar together with you. But the calendar is an instrument, a tool for working, a tool to reach a certain target. Which target? Let me give you two or three ideas which can facilitate your ideas and which you should take note of when you're organising your work. If we look at Article 65 bis, Rule 65 bis, you will see that there is a plan of work contained in that Rule, in Rule 65 bis, and the first thing that the parties must do in accordance with that Rule is to discuss between themselves, to organise exchanges between the parties so as to see whether they are in agreement as to facts and law. And in keeping with everything that Ms. Susan Somers said a moment ago, we must also take that into account, the possibility of having agreement, accord, and judicial notice of facts which have already been adjudicated. So that is why I say "law" as well, because it is only after having gone through this process of agreement and accord and seeing what we disagree on will you have identified the object of the process in trial itself. And with that stage in mind, you will be able to know what evidence and proof you require in order to prove your case, that is to say, to achieve the object of the trial, which witnesses you need, the witnesses that are coming to come to the courtroom to testify, the Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. witnesses who will have -- deposition witness following Rule 71 and 92 bis, and, finally, expert witnesses as well. But I'm going to discuss those under another category. And when we bring up the subject of witnesses, you must know which witnesses for which counts, which charges that are made, and how much time you estimate, how much time these will also take. When you do that, you come to another category of evidence and proof, and that is documents. And I would like to include into that category expert witnesses, because we're dealing with their reports as part of those documents. So whether it be Mr. Lukic or Mrs. Susan Somers - and I know they have had experience with this - we can present a report compiled by an expert witness. But if the other side, opposite party, does not accept that report, then they can call a second expert witness and a second -- that is to say, a second expert report. You know that these people, these professionals have schedules and are very often occupied elsewhere, so the reports are a good idea. Once you have the evidence and proof at this stage of the proceedings, what you have to do is to organise and plan for the opening of trial, and the Defence will be ready to state what the nature of its defence will, in fact, be and where the disagreements lie, where they do not agree with respect to law and facts. Therefore, the whole process has been sketched out, and then we can say that the trial go ahead on date "X" and it will end on date "Y," and it will be possible to envisage a calendar for the presentation of evidence and proof on the counts, and we will have an idea of how long the entire process will last, the Defence case and the Prosecution case. And we will be able to do that once we enter the stage -- and we'll have to do this with the Tribunal entering a phase where it will have six trials a day. So we will have to take into account the programme not as an objective but as an instrument, a tool for our work. But in order to do so, we shall have to respect it as much as possible. Although I know that programmes can always be modified and will have to be here and there, but if the parties work on the basis of those guidelines, I think we will achieve our target. So these are guidelines on my part, but I do think that you ought to focus on your agreements and your disagreements, on where you agree to the facts and the law and where you do not agree and the witnesses you need to prove your points. I think that is logical. And another guideline that I wish to put forward -- perhaps that more for Mr. Lukic's benefit, but I think that you must be aware of this: As you know, in the civil law system, the instruction phase, pre-trial phase is investigation, the Prosecution case and the Defence case. We, too, have different stages, but parties are quite autonomous as to how they build their case. That is to say, the Prosecutor will present their evidence, and that evidence will be cross-examined by the Defence. Then we open a second stage where the Defence presents its case with its evidence and the Prosecution has the right to cross-examine. I'm saying this because very often, I do understand, that the Defence is very anxious when the Prosecution case is being presented because it wishes to step into the Defence stage straight away. So I wanted to clarify this. And to do so, let me repeat once again, because this is an important point for to you understand, the first thing that you must do, your first preoccupation, your priority in your exchanges now, is not the number of witnesses or how many witnesses you're going to have, but you should focus on agreement on facts and law, in order to find - and I insist upon this - agreement on your points of disagreement, so as to define the object and target of the entire proceedings. Those, then, are some guidelines for you for the Status Conference and pre-trial stage. So once we have the preliminary motions filed, we will hold a Status Conference to operationalise what we have been talking about. We all know each other, I think, and the floor is always open for discussion. You have your legal officers who can act as liaison officers, and I'm always ready to receive you in my own offices, in chambers, to discuss any points you need to discuss. So please don't go into the stage of evidence and proof before you have gone into agreement and accord on your disagreements and disaccords, and I think that follows on from the logic of Rule 65 bis. So a plan of work is easy to devise and compile on the basis of Rule 65 bis. So I will leave you now, having given you those guidelines. But before we do so, I'm going to give you the opportunity to take the floor once more before I adjourn the meeting, to see if there are any practical matters which you wish to attend to. Ms. Susan Somers, what about you?

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. I would like to inform the Chamber that Mr. Lukic and I are working now on a draft protective-measures motion. I think I may have alluded to it earlier. That will be important because it will allow us to then remove or go past some of the typical redactions that I have spoken of earlier, and it will make it easier, I think, for preparation. Again, just as a reminder for the record, there is no new supporting material, so anything that comes out now will be toward the core of the case. And other than that, no. I very much appreciate the guidance the Chamber has given us. I do ask for clarification on the expert issue. When the Chamber said if there is a desire to cross-examine or we don't accept an expert, we can call another, is this in the same spirit as was done in Omarska where there was an expert, Kecmanovic, and rather than cross-examining, we presented a refutation, we refuted through our own expert? Is this the same type of scenario which the Chamber is envisioning? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. That was -- that is what I was thinking of precisely. In Omarska, I think we had a mixture. We had expert witnesses and you had 20 minutes to cross-examine, because you didn't accept some of the reasons. But I think in other cases, at least we had instances where the party that did not accept the -- a report made, a counter-report, a report by another expert to counterbalance the first one. And the Trial Chamber and the Judges are experts above experts, so it is up to the Chamber to decide and to see what weight they hold. Mr. Lukic, how about you? Would you like to take the floor?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, I know that I should organise my witnesses, my number of witnesses, my documents, but as I told you, I really don't know yet how many witnesses, I don't know yet how many documents, because I was working by myself on legal issues and I had only one investigator to go around, search, investigate. So I really hope that I will get a chance to get more investigators and to get one co-counsel. So when I know exactly how many documents and how many witnesses, I will be able to organise them, and that's why I really don't want to delay. I just want to organise. And that's why I estimated that I cannot begin before the second quarter of the next year. That's all really as explanation or as excuse, but that's how things stand now. Thanks.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Lukic, I have to tell you that you're going to have to anticipate a date like this kind because according to our work plan, we will have to complete the preliminary stage and be trial-ready towards February. But in any case, I think that the Registrar will take note of what you have said so that you will be given the human resources that you are in need of. And, Mr. Lukic, following from what I have said, I think it is quite possible as of now, and before you are assigned a co-counsel and a complete team, that you can sit down in pleasant surroundings with Ms. Susan Somers, for example, to look at the practical exercise of reading the indictment itself and to be able to see, "Well, I agree here and don't agree there. I reject this completely," and so on, or, "That paragraph is acceptable but not the other one," things like that. Bearing in mind that the important thing is, for you especially - and of course it's up to you to do your work - but to see your client's liability and responsibility with respect to the facts that are already known by the Tribunal and decisions that have been taken and in concrete terms, I think that it would be a good idea if you sit down to the negotiating table with the Prosecution and go into this exercise, which I think is a very useful one, to go through the indictment, to read it together, and to see how you stand, whether you agree or, at least to disagree -- or to agree on what you disagree on. It's too early - it's early days yet, Mr. Lukic - to be thinking of the number of witnesses. Let's take first things first. First of all, see what you do not agree with and then turn your mind to witnesses. But as I say, this is just a suggestion on my part as a Pre-Trial Judge, for me to structurise your meetings, to meet. To have something to drink is one thing, but to have a working meeting is another, and if you're going to have a working meeting, you must have an objective, a goal, and the goal that I'm giving you is to know first and foremost what the areas of law and fact are upon which you can agree. If you come to the conclusion that you don't have an agreement, then that also tells us where we stand and what we have to discuss. Very well. Having said that, thank you. I now turn to Dr. Stakic. Dr. Stakic, please stand.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I would like to give you an opportunity of giving you the floor. Would you like to say anything with respect to your conditions of detention and health? Is everything all right? Or do you have any questions you wish to raise, or problems?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour, for inquiring. I can say that I feel fairly well at the moment, and that I do not have anything special to bring up.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Please sit, Dr. Stakic. As you can see, we are doing our utmost to get the proceedings trial-ready as soon as possible and go ahead with your trial. The Prosecution, the Defence, and everybody else concerned will do their best to ensure that that happens. I don't think we have any other matters to attend to today. I wish you a pleasant evening and every success in your work, and I adjourn the meeting.
